Throughput is far below virtio-net TCP, which achieves approximately 400–600 MiB/s.
The DMA engine's PCI function is identified as `01:00.1` versus `01:00.3`, and this setting is stored in the EEPROM.

A live downstream port, `04:09.0`, is located at gen1 x0 and has no device connected behind it, corresponding to the M.2 riser.
The DMA engine has one channel per function (`PLX_8733_NUM_CHAN`), and `plx_dma_probe` adds a single embedded `plx_chan` to the list.
The maximum transfer size per descriptor is `PLX_DESC_SIZE_MASK` = 128 MiB − 1.

For DMA transfers, 64-byte alignment is required for the source, destination, and length (`PLX_DMA_ALIGN_SHIFT 6`), although misaligned transfers are functional but result in a rate-limited warning and performance drop.
Pipelined node-to-node throughput is up to 4423 MiB/s, which has been verified.
The DMA pipelined ring achieved a throughput of 2020 MiB/s in the node 1 $\leftrightarrow$ node 2 direction.
The DMA pipelined ring achieved a throughput of 4423 MiB/s in the node 2 $\leftrightarrow$ node 1 direction.
The DMA pipelined ring costs no CPU, unlike virtio at jumbo which saturates a core.
The ring's throughput varied by under 2%, whereas virtio at jumbo ranged from 7954–25583 Mbit/s.
The first working version of the payload fill managed only 2025 MiB/s because the sender refilled 512 KiB of local buffer with a CPU memset-style loop every iteration.
The BlockIO path is the only non-IP path successfully used from userspace so far.
The backend for the BlockIO FILE type performs `kernel_read` or `kernel_write` on the host file, then DMA to the card.
The backend for the BlockIO MEMORY type uses `vmalloc` on the host.
Hardware has 256 ALUT slots, which are divided by `num_ntbs`.
PCI IDs `0x2954` and `0x2955` (nodes 0/1) result in `num_ntbs = 2` and an ALUT base of `0x38000` (port 0) or `0x3a000` (port 1).
PCI ID `0x2956` (node 2) results in `num_ntbs = 1` and an ALUT base of `0x38000`.
The P580 reports 72 compute units, matching the datasheet's 72 EUs.
The real local memory on the P580 is 64 KB.
The P580 has a peak performance of approximately 1325 GFLOP/s FP32 per card.
At 79 GFLOP/s per GPU, the naive kernel is at approximately 6% of the P580's peak performance.
The naive kernel is purely memory bound, requiring one flop per four bytes.
Register blocking is the recommended next step to improve performance by making each work-item compute several outputs.
The symptom of the rtnl self-deadlock was that host pings, TCP 22 and 8006 accepted, and the Proxmox web served HTTP 200, but SSH never completed a login, and eventually the web UI went too.

The cause of the deadlock was that `register_netdevice()` invokes the netdev notifier chain with `rtnl` already held, and `rtnl_lock()` is not recursive, causing a `NETDEV_REGISTER` handler to self-deadlock.
The deadlock occurred inside the VOP workqueue and left `rtnl` held forever, causing everything needing `rtnl` to pile up behind it.
The issue only manifested during image work because the handler fires when a NIC registers while the module is loaded, which happens when a node reboots.
The issue was fixed on 2026-09-21 by modifying `apply_dev()` to take an explicit `rtnl_held` flag and use `netif_set_mtu()` instead of `dev_set_mtu()`.
The lesson that matters is that the host journal is persistent, and `journalctl -b -1 -k` shows the previous boot's kernel log, including the stack trace that preceded the wedge.
Every image now writes `/etc/vca-image-release`.
The script `/opt/vca-tools/verify_node_image.sh` can determine if a node is not what it claims.
The host masquerades `172.31.0.0/16` out of `vmbr0`, allowing nodes to ping `1.1.1.1` and the LAN, but only names fail.
The image build disables `systemd-resolved`, meaning the stub file in `/etc/resolv.conf` is never created.
`/sbin` IS `/usr/sbin` on any modern distro (usrmerge).
Process-per-request benchmarking silently penalises large models, and on this card the penalty is shared: each re-launch reloads the model over the same host BlockIO path.
The host does not run Intel's VCASS 2.3.26 modules.
The host runs a third-party forward-port, plus a local hand-built patch to its most important module.
The source for the installed driver stack is [`chainsx/intel-vca2-dkms`] at `edb3e51`.
The packages installed are `daemon-vca`, `vca2-host`, and `vca2-vcass-modules-dkms`, all version `2.3.26+ubuntu24.04.10`.
The host stack was built for kernels `7.0.2-6-pve` and `7.0.14-17-pve`, with 17 modules each.
Stock `plx87xx` cannot build against the installed kernels because both kernels define `struct dma_map_ops` with `.map_phys` / `.unmap_phys` and no `.map_page` / `.unmap_page`.
The host driver stack is documented in HOST_STACK.md.
The fix (`put_device()`) for the `kfree` after a failed `device_register()` issue was applied consistently across all five buses.
The branch where `BLK_STS_RESOURCE` with no queue kick risks a stall is unreachable by construction because `queue_depth = REQ_RING_SIZE - 1 = 2047` equals the ring's usable capacity.
The `plx87xx_dma/` directory is byte-identical to Intel's.
The project has been driving this card continuously since 2026-09-19.
Anything reported upstream should name the local `plx87xx` patch because the project has validated the port plus a modification.

The rtnl self-deadlock is the root cause of three host wedges, occurring when a network device registers while the module is loaded, causing the host to become unresponsive.
The cause of the host wedges is due to the `register_netdevice()` function invoking the netdev notifier chain with `rtnl` already held, resulting in a deadlock.
The deadlock occurs inside the VOP workqueue, causing the sshd process to stop completing logins.
The issue only surfaces during image work, as the handler fires when a NIC registers while the module is loaded, which is when a node reboots.

The issue can be fixed by using the `apply_dev()` function with an explicit `rtnl_held` flag and the `netif_set_mtu()` function instead of `dev_set_mtu()` (which acquires `rtnl`), as this change resolves the deadlock and prevents the host from wedging.
The host journal is persistent and provides valuable information for troubleshooting, including the previous boot's kernel log, which can reveal the stack trace that preceded the wedge.

Both installed host kernels define `struct dma_map_ops` with `.map_phys` / `.unmap_phys` and no `.map_page` / `.unmap_page`.
The `plx87xx` module does not merely call the DMA API — it provides a `dma_map_ops` table, redirecting the synthetic VOP device's DMA onto the real PLX PCI device.
